Formulation:
Maria presents with a first episode of acute, severe, unilateral (left-sided) headache, blurred vision with zigzag lines, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, consistent with migraine with aura. Her family history (mother with migraine) supports this diagnosis. The event has triggered significant health anxiety, with fears of brain tumor and stroke despite absence of neurological deficits. Predisposing factors include family history of migraine. Precipitating factors involve the sudden onset of unfamiliar neurological symptoms. Perpetuating factor includes ongoing health anxiety possibly linked to previous medical history. Protective factors are insight into her anxiety, appropriate help-seeking, and good engagement with medical advice.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Migraine with Aura (with secondary health anxiety)
- Patient Goal(s): Relief from acute headache symptoms; reassurance regarding absence of life-threatening condition
- Clinical Goal(s): Symptom resolution; address health anxiety; ensure understanding of migraine management and alarm features; arrange follow-up for safety and potential further assessment
- Actions (Patient): Take recommended medications (ibuprofen, anti-sickness medications – dose/route/frequency not documented); monitor symptoms; attend follow-up assessment as planned; notify clinic if symptoms worsen or do not improve; apply medically-advised self-care (rest, fluids, avoid screens)
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provided diagnosis explanation and education regarding migraine; recommended medication strategy; advised on red flag symptoms and when to seek urgent review; arranged in-person follow-up for neurological assessment if symptoms persist or worsen; provided reassurance regarding differential diagnoses

Secondary Problem: Health Anxiety
- Patient Goal(s): Understand causes of symptoms; reduce fear of serious illness
- Clinical Goal(s): Reassure and educate regarding likely benign nature of current symptoms while maintaining vigilance for serious pathology; encourage ongoing communication regarding health concerns
- Actions (Patient): Voice concerns appropriately; follow medical advice; return for follow-up if anxious or symptomatic
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide explanations normalizing migraine onset at any age; clarify rationale for differential diagnoses; encourage patient contact if further concerns arise

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Probable diagnosis of migraine (features, triggers, course); family history; acute management; duration of symptoms; importance of follow-up for unresolved or worsening symptoms; health anxiety normalized and addressed; alarm features discussed (worsening pain, new neurological symptoms, persistent vomiting)
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increasing headache severity; development of neurological deficits (weakness, sensory changes, speech disturbance); persistent or intractable vomiting; changes in consciousness or confusion
- Coping Strategies: Rest in low-stimulation environment; medication as advised; tailored reassurance about prognosis

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Not recorded
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded
- Review Date: Not recorded

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine with aura — High likelihood: Fits acute, unilateral moderate-severe headache, visual aura, nausea/vomiting, and family history. No focal neurological deficit.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage — Low likelihood: Sudden onset could suggest SAH, but pain not maximal or ‘worst ever’, no neck stiffness or neuro deficit.
- Ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke — Low likelihood: Sudden onset and visual change, but absence of focal neuro deficit, gait or speech abnormality.
